title: 3.6.17 Pass by Value/Reference
description: Eight multiple-choice questions on primitives vs objects, mutation vs reassignment, side effects, and defensive copying. Checked instantly.

questions.question: When you pass a primitive (a number, string, or boolean) to a function, what does the function receive?
options: A pointer to the same value, so the function can change your variable
The name of your variable instead of its value
A copy of the value, so changing it leaves your original untouched
Nothing until the function asks for it
questions.explanation: Primitives are passed by value: the function gets its own copy. Reassigning that copy cannot reach back to your variable. The first option describes objects, not primitives.

questions.question: When you pass an array to a function, what does the function receive?
options: A full copy of every element, kept separate from yours
A copy of the reference: an address pointing at the same array
A read-only view that cannot be changed
A new empty array to fill in
questions.explanation: An array is an object, so the function gets a copy of the reference. Both names point at one array, which is why a push inside the function shows up outside it.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: undefined
An error: you cannot change a parameter
questions.explanation: x is a number, so update received a copy. `val = val + 1` reassigned the copy to 6 and then the function ended. x never moved, so it prints 5.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: undefined
questions.explanation: `nums[i] = ...` writes into the shared array, which is mutation rather than reassignment. The caller sees every change, so scores becomes [11, 21, 31].

questions.question: Which line mutates an object rather than reassigning a name?
options: num = 4
label = "new"
arr.push(4)
questions.explanation: `arr.push(4)` changes the contents of the array both names point at, so everyone holding a reference sees it. The other three lines point one name at a different value and nothing else moves.

questions.question: What happens when you run this? `const items = ["pen"]; items.push("notebook");`
options: It throws: you cannot change a const array
It runs fine; const locks the binding, not the contents
It runs but silently drops the new item
It makes a copy of items first, then pushes
questions.explanation: const promises the name will always point at this same array. Pushing does not change which array that is, so it is allowed. The line that would throw is `items = ["eraser"]`, because that reassigns the binding.

questions.question: What is a side effect?
options: Any value a function returns
An error thrown inside a function
A change a function makes that outlives the call and is visible outside it
A parameter with a default value
questions.explanation: A side effect is a lasting change, most often mutating an object the function was passed. It is not automatically bad — sortScores exists to reorder — but an unexpected one is a hard bug.

questions.question: You make a copy of an object with `{...original}` and then push into a nested array inside the copy. What happens to the original?
options: The original's nested array changes too, because the copy is only one level deep
Nothing: the copy is completely separate
It throws, because you cannot copy an object that holds an array
The original becomes undefined
questions.explanation: Spread makes a shallow copy: the outer object is new, but any nested array or object inside is still shared. Change the nested array and both see it. structuredClone makes a copy that goes all the way down.
